chapters.title: Chapter 1: From Power Law to Portfolio Strategy

lessons.title: Quantifying the Power Law: Modeling Returns Across a Real Portfolio

body.text: A portfolio of twenty average startups is not diversification in the mutual fund sense. It is a lottery machine, and your only job is to hold enough correctly sized tickets to be in the room when one of them pays out fifty times your money.

children.text: If you have come from the introductory angel investing course, you already know the story: most startups fail, a handful return your capital, and a rare few return so much that they carry the entire portfolio. That is the power law told qualitatively. This lesson tells it with numbers. You will build an actual outcome distribution for a hypothetical portfolio, compute its portfolio MOIC (multiple on invested capital), and see exactly how much of the return comes from exactly how few positions. Everything else in this course, sizing, diversification, reserves, follow-ons, is a set of decisions you make in response to this math. Skip the math and you are just guessing at each of them.
The Outcome Distribution Behind Every Angel Portfolio

markDefs.definition: Multiple on Invested Capital: total proceeds received from an investment (or a portfolio) divided by the total capital put in. A MOIC of 3x means you got back three rupees for every rupee invested, across the life of the investment, before adjusting for time or IRR.

children.text: Take a portfolio of 20 startups, one cheque of ₹5 lakh each, ₹1 crore deployed in total. You will not know in advance which position does what, that is the entire point of building a portfolio instead of picking one stock. But you can model a realistic spread of outcomes and work out what it does to your

. The table below is illustrative, not a prediction for any specific portfolio, but the shape of it, a large cluster of total losses, a middling cluster near 1x, and a thin tail of large winners, matches what shows up again and again in early-stage investing.

body.caption: A hypothetical 20-startup portfolio, ₹5 lakh per cheque
P(i) = proceeds from investment i, C(i) = capital invested in i, n = number of positions in the portfolio

children.text: Add up the Proceeds column: ₹0 + ₹25,00,000 + ₹45,00,000 + ₹50,00,000 + ₹2,50,00,000 = ₹3,70,00,000. Total capital invested was ₹1,00,00,000. Portfolio MOIC = 3,70,00,000 divided by 1,00,00,000 = 3.7x. Fifteen of twenty positions, three quarters of the portfolio by count, returned 1x or less. The portfolio still turned ₹1 crore into ₹3.7 crore, entirely because of the two winners at the bottom of the table.

body.text: Remove that one 50x position from the table and replace it with another total loss instead. Proceeds fall from ₹3.70 crore to ₹1.20 crore, and portfolio MOIC drops from 3.7x to 1.2x, barely ahead of the capital you put in. Nineteen out of twenty investment decisions in this portfolio were, in hindsight, close to irrelevant to the outcome. That is not a flaw in the strategy. It is the strategy.

This does not mean you can identify the outlier in advance and concentrate on it. Nobody, however experienced, reliably picks the 50x company out of a shortlist at the cheque-writing stage. The lesson is the opposite: because you cannot identify it in advance, you need enough positions, sized sensibly, that the eventual winner (whichever one it turns out to be) is actually large enough within your portfolio to matter.

body.title: Compute a Portfolio MOIC Yourself
body.prompt: You build a 10-startup portfolio with equal ₹10 lakh cheques, ₹1 crore deployed in total. At exit: 5 positions return 0x, 3 return 1x, 1 returns 5x, and 1 returns 20x. What is the portfolio MOIC? Answer as a multiple, e.g. 2.5 for 2.5x.
body.explanation: Proceeds: 5 × ₹0 = ₹0; 3 × 1 × ₹10L = ₹30L; 1 × 5 × ₹10L = ₹50L; 1 × 20 × ₹10L = ₹200L. Total proceeds = ₹280L (₹2.8 crore) against ₹1 crore invested, so MOIC = 2.8x. Here too, the single 20x position (₹200L of the ₹280L in proceeds) supplied over 71% of the return.

children.text: Why Position Count and Position Size Both Matter

Two portfolios can hold the same 20 companies and still produce very different MOICs, purely because of how the cheques were sized. If the ₹5 lakh that would have gone into the eventual 50x winner had instead been capped at ₹1 lakh, on the theory that it looked too speculative to size normally, that position would have returned ₹50,00,000 instead of ₹2,50,00,000. The portfolio's proceeds would have fallen by ₹2,00,00,000, and MOIC would have dropped from 3.7x to roughly 1.9x. Under-sizing your eventual winner is functionally the same mistake as missing it altogether, just a smaller version of it. Chapter 2 builds the full math for deciding cheque size and ownership targets; the point to take from this lesson is that sizing decisions are not a side detail, they multiply directly into the number that matters.

columns.label: Diversification as Noise Reduction (Public Markets Logic)
points: Spreading 20 to 30 listed stocks across sectors to smooth volatility
Every holding is expected to contribute somewhere near the portfolio average
Goal: a stable, predictable return path with a tight distribution of outcomes

columns.label: Diversification as Power Law Capture (Angel Logic)
points: Spreading capital across enough companies to statistically make room for one true outlier
Most positions are expected, by design, to return close to zero
Goal: maximise the odds of catching the outlier and its payoff, not smooth the average

children.text: This is not only a modeling exercise. Info Edge, the NSE and BSE-listed parent of Naukri.com, wrote one of the earliest cheques into Zomato back in 2010. By the time Zomato listed on the Indian exchanges in 2021, Info Edge's cumulative stake was worth well over ₹10,000 crore. Indian financial media has reported the resulting multiple on Info Edge's original investment anywhere from roughly 200x to over 300x, depending on which funding tranche is used as the base and how later dilution and part-sales are treated, so treat the exact figure as directional rather than a precise, single number. What is not in dispute is the shape: one position, held inside a broader portfolio of Info Edge's other startup bets, generated returns on a scale that dwarfed everything else Info Edge had funded around the same time.

body.title: Pushback From a 'Back Conviction, Not Spray and Pray' Angel
body.scenario: You have ₹75 lakh to deploy as an angel investor over the next 18 months. A well-regarded operator-turned-angel tells you: "Don't spray and pray across 20 companies. Back your best 5 ideas with ₹15 lakh each, and go deep on conviction."
body.prompt: Using what you now know about outcome distributions and portfolio MOIC, how do you respond?
body.modelAnswer: Five positions is too few shots on goal for power law math to work in your favour, regardless of how good your judgment is. Even experienced angels cannot reliably identify the outlier in advance, it is a statistical structure problem, not a stock-picking skill problem. With only 5 positions there is a real chance none of them lands the 10x-plus outcome that a portfolio of 20 to 30 has structural room for. The better response is to keep enough positions that the power law has somewhere to show up, size each cheque so a single winner still moves the needle rather than getting diluted across too many tiny bets, and hold back capital to follow on into the 1 or 2 names that show real signal after the first round, instead of committing full conviction sizing on day one across only 5 names.

body.title: How This Compares to Real Venture Capital Data

children.text: A widely cited analysis by Correlation Ventures, covering more than 21,000 US venture financings between 2004 and 2013, found that roughly 65% of financings returned less than the capital invested, and only about 2.5% returned 10x or more. That thin slice of 10x-plus outcomes accounted for the large majority of aggregate returns across the entire dataset, the same lopsided shape you just built in the 20-startup table above, at much larger scale.

content.text: The Correlation Ventures figures are US venture capital data spanning multiple stages, not an India-specific angel dataset. Indian angel investing does not yet have a public dataset of comparable size and rigor. Use these numbers as a directional sanity check on the shape of the distribution, not as an Indian-market statistic.

points: Power law outcomes are not something a portfolio avoids by diversifying, they are the reason you diversify in the first place
A portfolio's MOIC is overwhelmingly decided by its one or two best positions, not by its average position
Losing all or most of your capital on the majority of individual investments is the expected, designed outcome of this strategy, not a sign it has failed
Position sizing matters as much as position count, a winner that is sized too small still caps your portfolio's overall return
Real-world outcomes like Info Edge's Zomato investment show the scale a single position can reach, even where the exact reported multiple varies by source
